# OWASP ZAP

The Zed Attack Proxy — an open-source web application security scanner maintained by OWASP volunteers,
usable both as an automated scanner and as a manual testing proxy. It carries labs 13 and 14 of
[[cybersecurity-engineering-laboratories]], alongside Burp Suite and Postman, against the deliberately
vulnerable OWASP Juice Shop.

## The proxy is the whole idea

Configure the browser to route through ZAP and every request is captured **after it leaves the
browser**. The tester can then read it, modify it, and forward it.

The lab reports name the structural point directly: this is a
[[man-in-the-middle-attack]] where the tester holds both roles. And the consequence is the single most
important finding in lab 13:

**Every validation performed only in client-side JavaScript is advisory.** Length limits, format
checks, hidden fields, disabled controls, price values in a form — all of it is editable in the proxy
after the client-side code has run and before the server sees it. Client-side validation is a UX
feature; it is not a security control. Everything that matters must be re-checked server-side.

## What the labs used it for

| Capability | Exercised on |
|---|---|
| Intercepting proxy | modifying requests to bypass client-side validation |
| Spider / passive scan | mapping the application surface |
| Active scan | automated probing for known vulnerability classes |
| Request replay / manual edit | broken authentication and broken access control, including object-identifier enumeration |
| Fuzzer | substituting payload lists into a parameter position |

The vulnerability classes themselves are covered on [[web-application-injection]] — injection, broken
authentication, broken access control, improper input validation, security misconfiguration — without
any payload strings.

## Where the labs stopped short

The fuzzing exercises did not complete. The lab-13 report records the fuzzer not running and the
author following the task sheet, then outside instructions, without success; the lab-14 report records
a local instance that would not start and a task the author records not understanding.

**TODO:** whether these were completed later is unrecorded. `confidence: low` on the completeness of
the tooling exercises; `confidence: high` on the proxy-interception findings, which the reports
document working.

## Automated scanning is a floor, not a ceiling

Worth stating because the tool invites the opposite belief. An active scan finds known patterns:
reflected inputs, missing headers, default files, obvious injection points. It does not find business
logic flaws, and broken access control — the class the lab exercised most successfully — is almost
entirely invisible to it, because *the request is well-formed and the response is a valid 200*. Only
someone who knows which identifier belongs to whom can tell that the answer was wrong. The manual
proxy work, not the scanner, is where the lab's real findings came from.
